content: The use of misoprostol for self-administration by women after childbirth to prevent postpartum hemorrhage, delivered by lay health workers (LHWs), has become a common practice. The World Health Organization (WHO) established a Guidance Development Group (GDG) for this project, which included staff from various WHO departments such as Reproductive Health and Research (RHR), Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (MCA), HIV/AIDS, Nutrition, and Human Resources for Health. This group reviewed stakeholder consultation materials, provided advice and guidance on key questions and outcomes, and participated in a guidance scoping meeting. The GDG contributed throughout the guidance development process. A WHO Technical Secretariat was also formed, consisting of a Lead Technical Officer from WHO and two researchers from the Norwegian Knowledge Centre for the Health Services. The Secretariat supported the development of the guidance, coordinated research syntheses and other necessary materials, and led the creation of the guidance document. Stakeholder consultation to identify critical questions and outcomes was conducted in two stages: an online discussion via the WHO Knowledge Gateway (November 8–16, 2010) and a guidance scoping meeting. Contributions were received from a diverse group of policymakers, program managers, researchers, and healthcare providers, representing 33 countries. The discussion focused on three themes: optimizing health worker roles at the primary care level, at the community level, and the roles of trained traditional birth attendants (tTBAs). Questions and issues raised by 187 participants were summarized and further evaluated during the scoping meeting. The guidance scoping meeting involved an international panel of stakeholders, including midwives, obstetricians, associate clinicians, neonatologists, researchers, and experts in research synthesis and healthcare programs. Together, the GDG and the Technical Secretariat made decisions to facilitate discussions and ensure the feasibility of addressing guidance questions within the available time and resources. These decisions included defining health worker cadres, identifying relevant recipients of care, and selecting clinical interventions for optimization based on evidence of effectiveness in improving maternal and newborn health outcomes. Interventions were excluded if they could be safely delivered by less-trained cadres or if they required specialist training and skills. Examples of excluded interventions included the promotion of companionship during labor by auxiliary nurse midwives and neonatal resuscitation by non-specialist doctors. The evidence retrieval process considered three main types of evidence: (1) effectiveness of interventions delivered by specific cadres based on randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (n-RCTs), controlled before-and-after studies (CBAs), interrupted time series (ITS), and cohort studies; (2) qualitative studies on factors affecting the implementation of programs to optimize health worker tasks and roles; and (3) country case studies on large-scale human resource programs. Cochrane systematic reviews were the primary source of evidence for intervention effectiveness, and where reviews were outdated, authors were invited to update them. Non-Cochrane reviews were included only if no Cochrane reviews were available. Qualitative evidence reviews focused on factors affecting task shifting in midwifery programs, lay health worker programs, nurse-doctor substitution programs, and the acceptability of compact, prefilled auto-disable devices (CPADs). These reviews included studies using qualitative methods for data collection and analysis, conducted in community or primary healthcare settings, and focused on the experiences and attitudes of key stakeholders such as healthcare providers, program recipients, managers, and policymakers. Large-scale programs to address human resource deficits in health, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), were reviewed to identify factors, policies, and contexts affecting their implementation. These programs aimed to optimize the roles and tasks of healthcare providers to maximize the existing workforce's capacity. Two reviews were conducted: one on scaling up maternal and newborn health (MNH) programs and another on scaling up contraceptive delivery programs. Eligible programs were national or state-wide, publicly funded, and implemented for at least five years. Evaluation reports and studies were gathered through key informants, electronic databases, and web searches. A cross-cutting analysis of findings from qualitative studies and country case studies was undertaken to deepen understanding of factors affecting the implementation of task and role optimization programs. This analysis evaluated opinions on optimizing healthcare provider roles to improve maternal and newborn health in LMICs and the implications of such optimizations. Text relevant to task shifting was extracted and analyzed using qualitative thematic analysis to identify key views and experiences.
